statement: A written incident management procedure runs from detection through closure, and each incident role has a named person with contact details. The procedure and roles are shared with everyone who has a part in them. The plan is exercised at least yearly, for example with a tabletop, so that people know what to do when an incident happens. The procedure, the role list and the exercise records are the proof.
why_asked: Without a tested plan and named people, the first hours of an incident are lost to confusion about who decides and who calls whom. Consultants want to see that the plan is alive, not a document written once for an audit.
how_to_ask: Ask how an incident would be led tomorrow and ask to see the plan and the role list. Then ask when the plan was last rehearsed and who took part. Example probe: "If a ransomware alert came in tonight, who would take charge, and where do I find their phone number?"
question: Does your organization keep an exercised incident management plan with named roles and contact details?
expected_evidence: Incident management procedure or incident response plan; incident role list with named people and contact details; communication record showing the plan reached those involved; tabletop or other exercise report with attendance; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: A current procedure covers detection, reporting, triage, response, communication and closure. Each role has a named person and a reachable contact, and a deputy. The plan was shared with those involved and exercised within the last year, with actions from the exercise followed up.
test: Obtain the procedure and role list and check that every stage from detection to closure is covered and every role has a named person with contact details. Select the most recent exercise and confirm it took place within the last year and that attendees match the role list. Pass if the procedure is complete, the roles are named and the exercise is recent.
baseline_risk: Incidents are handled ad hoc, response is slow and inconsistent, and nobody can be reached when it matters.
key_settings: base: incident plan exercised at least yearly

statement: Written criteria and severity levels decide when a security event becomes an incident. Every logged event is assessed against those criteria, and the decision and the severity are recorded. This keeps real incidents from being missed and minor events from flooding response. The classification matrix and the triage records are the proof.
why_asked: If nothing defines when an event is an incident, serious events get dismissed and notification clocks start late. Consultants test whether triage decisions are recorded, not just whether a matrix exists.
how_to_ask: Ask to see the written criteria, then pick a few logged events and ask to see the decision on each. Example probe: "Show me an event from last quarter that you decided was not an incident, and the record of why."
question: Does your organization assess logged security events against written criteria to decide whether each is an incident and how severe it is?
expected_evidence: Incident classification and severity matrix; event log export; event triage records showing the decision on each event; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: Written criteria define incident and severity levels in terms staff can apply. Each logged event carries a recorded assessment, a decision and a severity where it was escalated, with the name of the assessor and a timestamp.
test: Check that the written criteria define an incident and severity levels. Sample logged events across the review period, including some closed as not an incident, and confirm each has a recorded assessment and decision. Pass if the criteria exist and every sampled event has a recorded decision consistent with them.
baseline_risk: Real incidents are missed or downgraded, and response effort is spent on the wrong events.

statement: Every incident is handled under documented procedures for containment, eradication, recovery and escalation. The steps taken are recorded as the work happens, and each incident is closed only after recovery is confirmed. This limits damage and leaves a trail that shows the response was controlled. The response procedures and the incident records are the proof.
why_asked: A response that is not recorded cannot be repeated, reviewed or defended later. Consultants look for incidents that stayed open, or closed without evidence that recovery was confirmed.
how_to_ask: Ask for the response procedures, then pick a recent incident and walk the record from first alert to closure. Example probe: "For your last significant incident, show me when it was contained, when it was recovered and who signed off the closure."
question: Does your organization respond to every incident under documented procedures through to a recorded closure?
expected_evidence: Incident response procedures covering containment, eradication, recovery and escalation; incident register or log; sampled incident records showing steps taken and closure; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: Procedures set out containment, eradication, recovery and escalation steps with decision points. Every incident has a record of the steps actually taken, who took them and when, and a closure entry that confirms recovery.
test: Check that the procedures cover containment, eradication, recovery and escalation. Sample incidents from the review period, weighting toward the highest severity, and confirm each record shows the documented steps were followed and the incident was formally closed. Pass if the procedures are complete and every sampled record shows steps and closure.
baseline_risk: Incidents are contained slowly or not at all, steps are lost, and the organization cannot show what it did.

statement: The people who may notify authorities and other outside parties about an incident are named, and a timeline is set for each kind of reportable event. When an incident triggers a legal or contractual duty, notification is made in time, with the date and recipient recorded. This keeps the organization out of penalties and keeps customers and regulators informed. The notification procedure and the incident notification records are the proof.
why_asked: Late or unauthorized notification is often the costliest part of an incident, through fines and lost trust. Consultants check that someone is empowered to act and that the duties are known before an incident happens.
how_to_ask: Ask who can pick up the phone to a regulator or a customer and where the deadlines are written down. Then ask for an incident that triggered a duty. Example probe: "Which of your incidents last year had to be reported outside, and how did you show it went out on time?"
question: Does your organization notify authorities and other parties of incidents within the required time where a legal or contractual duty applies?
expected_evidence: Notification procedure naming who may contact authorities and the timelines for reportable events; register of legal and contractual notification duties; incident records showing notifications sent with dates and recipients; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: The procedure names the people who may notify and the timeline for each duty, drawn from a maintained register of legal and contractual duties. Every incident record shows whether a duty applied, and where it did, the date, recipient and content of the notification.
test: Check that the procedure names who may notify and sets timelines for reportable events. Sample incidents from the review period that triggered a legal or contractual duty and compare notification dates against the required time. Pass if the authority is named and every sampled notification was made within the required time.
baseline_risk: Notification duties are missed or made by unauthorized people, exposing the organization to penalties and loss of trust.

statement: Every significant incident gets a recorded post-incident review. The review produces control improvements, which are tracked through the change or risk process until each one is complete. This makes the organization less likely to repeat the same failure. The review records and the improvement tracker are the proof.
why_asked: Without a review, the same incident repeats and the cost of the first one is wasted. Consultants look for improvements that were actually completed, not only listed.
how_to_ask: Ask which incidents counted as significant last year, then ask for the review of one and the actions that came out of it. Example probe: "What changed in your controls after your last significant incident, and where can I see that it was finished?"
question: Does your organization review significant incidents and track the resulting control improvements to completion?
expected_evidence: Incident procedure section requiring a post-incident review; post-incident review reports; improvement tracker or change records linked to incidents; risk assessment updates; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: The procedure defines significant incidents and requires a review for each. Reviews record root cause and agreed improvements with owners and dates. The improvements appear in a tracker and show as completed, with the risk assessment updated where needed.
test: Check that the procedure requires a post-incident review for significant incidents. Take the significant incidents in the review period and confirm each has a recorded review, then trace at least one resulting improvement through the tracker to completion. Pass if every significant incident was reviewed and the traced improvement was completed.
baseline_risk: The organization repeats the same incidents because root causes are never fixed.

statement: A procedure sets how evidence of security events is identified, collected, acquired and preserved, including a chain of custody. When evidence is collected during an incident, an evidence-handling record is completed. This keeps the evidence usable for investigation, disciplinary action or legal proceedings. The evidence-handling procedure and the custody records are the proof.
why_asked: Evidence that was altered or has no custody record may be rejected in legal or disciplinary action. Consultants check that the people handling incidents know how to preserve evidence before they are under pressure.
how_to_ask: Ask how a laptop or a log set would be preserved from a compromised server, and ask for the record from the last time it happened. Example probe: "When you last pulled disk images or logs during an incident, who handled them and where is that written down?"
question: Does your organization preserve evidence of security events with a documented chain of custody?
expected_evidence: Evidence-handling procedure covering identification, collection, acquisition and preservation; chain-of-custody or evidence-handling records for incidents where evidence was collected; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: A procedure explains how evidence is identified, collected, acquired and preserved, with custody transfer steps and secure storage. Each collection has a record showing what was taken, by whom, when and where it is kept.
test: Check that the procedure covers identification, collection, acquisition, preservation and chain of custody. Select incidents in the review period where evidence was collected and confirm each has a custody or handling record. Pass if the procedure is complete and every sampled collection has a record.
baseline_risk: Evidence is lost or tainted, so the cause cannot be proven and legal or disciplinary action fails.

statement: A current list is kept of the authorities the organization may need to contact, such as the data protection regulator, the national incident response team, law enforcement and the sector regulator. The list says when each is contacted. It is verified at least yearly so that contacts are right when an incident happens. The contact list and its review record are the proof.
why_asked: A stale list wastes time during an incident when a regulator or law enforcement must be reached quickly. Consultants check that the list is dated and that someone owns it.
how_to_ask: Ask to see the contact list and the date it was last checked. Example probe: "When did someone last call or email each authority on this list to confirm the details still work?"
question: Does your organization keep a current list of relevant authorities and verify it regularly?
expected_evidence: Authority contact list showing which authority is contacted and when; record of the last verification or update; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: The list names each relevant authority with a current contact point and the trigger for contacting it. It carries a review date within the last year and an owner, and changes are recorded.
test: Obtain the contact list and check it names the relevant authorities and when each is contacted. Confirm the review date shows it was verified or updated within the last year. Pass if the list is complete for the organization's sector and the verification is recent.
baseline_risk: Staff cannot reach the right authority quickly during an incident, which delays reporting and support.
key_settings: base: authority contact list verified at least yearly

statement: A channel, such as a mailbox, portal or hotline, is published where personnel report observed or suspected security events as soon as they notice them. Personnel are told what to report and how, through awareness material and onboarding. This surfaces events that tools do not detect. The published channel, the awareness content and the reported events in the incident log are the proof.
why_asked: Staff often see the first signs of an incident, such as a phishing email or a lost device, and will not report them if they do not know how. Consultants look for evidence that people actually use the channel.
how_to_ask: Ask staff how they would report a suspicious email and see whether their answer matches the published channel. Then ask for events reported by personnel. Example probe: "How many events did staff report last quarter, and how fast were they logged?"
question: Does your organization give personnel a published channel to report security events promptly and tell them what to report?
expected_evidence: Published reporting channel description in the policy or intranet; awareness material saying what to report and how; incident log entries reported by personnel with timestamps; covering the last annual cycle.
good_looks_like: A single, well known channel is published to all personnel. Awareness content explains what to report with examples. The incident log shows events reported by personnel with short gaps between noticing and logging.
test: Confirm the channel is defined and published to personnel and that awareness material states what to report and how. Sample events in the incident log reported by personnel during the review period and check the timestamps show timely reporting. Pass if the channel and guidance exist and sampled events were reported and logged promptly.
baseline_risk: Early warning signs go unreported, so incidents are found late and cause more damage.
